data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is a combined radiative-advective obstruction: street canyon geometry traps both longwave radiation and stagnant air, so on calm nights the boundary layer decouples from the regional flow and the air\u2013surface temperature difference grows; the cross-city gap scales inversely with wind speed and sky view, making it most pronounced in dense, tall cities during calm conditions.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If wind speed were found to have no measurable effect on nocturnal UHI intensity, the advective obstruction component would be overturned.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If rural and urban surfaces had identical sky view factors and aerodynamic roughness, this mechanism would not produce a gap.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the nocturnal UHI were strongest in cities with the highest wind speeds, this mechanism would be falsified.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Nighttime cooling requires both radiative loss to the sky and turbulent removal of cooled air. The urban canyon geometry simultaneously reduces sky view (cutting longwave cooling) and increases aerodynamic roughness (slowing wind, cutting sensible and latent heat removal). The single mechanism is geometric obstruction of cooling fluxes. The gap scales with building height and built density, which set both the radiative and advective obstruction, and is strongest when wind speed is low.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
